Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That there shall be a board known as the Canadian Farm Loan Board which shall be a body politic and cc-rporate consisting of four members, one of whom shall be the Minister of Finance and the other three shall be appointed by the Governor in Council and of the latter one shall be designated by the Canadian Farm Loan Commissioners.
That the board shall issue farm loan bonds to make long term loans to farmers, and the government of Canada shalll provide initial capital for the board to an amount not exceeding five million dollars and subscribe an amount of 5 per cent of the capital stock as loans are made by the board.

The government o>f each province in which loans are made shall be required to subscribe to the capital stock of the board as loans are made in such province an amount equal to 5 per cent of the said loans and each borrower an amount of 5 per cent of his loan payable at the time the loan is made. The loans shall be made on the security of first mortgage cn farm lands; the interest rate shall be such a rate in excess of the interest payable on the farm loan bonds as is sufficient to provide for the expenses of operation; the farm loan bonds shall be legal investments and may be .purchased by the Minister of Finance provided that the amount of such bonds held by him shall not at any time exceed $15,000,000; and the amount of any payment by the government of Canada on account of capital of the board or as payment for farm loan bonds purchased shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund on the authority of the Governor in Council.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the House.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved:
That rule 10 of the House of Commons relating to the appointment of the select standing committees of the House be amended by adding to the select standing committees of the House for the present session a select standing committee on Railways and Shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government, to which will be referred the estimates of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Merchant Marine for the present session, for consideration and for report to the House, provided, however, that nothing in this resolution shall be construed to curtail in any way the full right of discussion in committee of Supply; and that the said committee consist of Messrs. Bell (St. Antoine), Boys, Campbell, Fiset, Clark, Drayton, Dunning, Euler, Harris, Heaps, Jelliff, Jones, Johnston, Power, Robichaud.

I oppose the motion. I do not think it is in the public interest that this committee should usurp the rights of parliament. The committee should not be appointed. The National railway is a public utility which should be operated from the commercial aspect and the country has elected 245 members of parliament as directors to see it is run properly.
We appointed a committee last year to go into the estimates of this particular railway and its operations from the commercial standpoint. The same special committee was appointed two or three years ago and what did it do? It met once in a while. The members of the House could not get any information about the operation of the road unless they were on the committee. Then a

National Railways and Shipping Committee
report was presented in the dying hours of the session. Last year the matter was taken up at a quarter past one in the morning of the day the House prorogued. This railway does not pay interest on the debt due the country; $42,000,000 interest is entered as a bookkeeping item. It is a frozen asset. When we ask questions about the operation of the railway and its finances we are told that it is not in the public interest to divulge information. The Canadian Pacific Railway can get it though. We know the salary of the Governor General and the salary of Sir Henry Thornton and the cabinet, but when we ask for the salaries of some of the American imported officials they say the question is out of order. I think the Canadian National Railways should be operated according to business principles free of politics and should be put on a paying basis. From the president down the men on the Canadian Pacific are Cahadians, but the National Railways are importing men from the United States and you do not know who they are, what their contracts are or what expenses they incur.
Let us take another case of public ownership, the Hydro-Electric Power Commission, with an investment of $262,000,000. Every year Sir Adam Beck, the late minister, had to meet the House and explain his estimates and he laid all the cards on the table. The Minister of Railway and Canals has had his functions taken away from him and the portfolio might as well be abolished. The railway commission has taken away part of the functions of the Minister of Railways in regard to rates and Sir Henry Thornton has taken away his other functions so that the portfolio itself as I say, might as well be done away with. The other day we asked for an agreement regarding the operation of the National Railways and the giving away of a public franchise of the Grand Trunk Railway on the streets of Detroit including Woodward avenue. Where is that agreement? Will the minister bring it down as he promised? No. On the other hand, Governor GroeSbeck called the Michigan legislature on the Fourth of February last and it held a special session to consider that agreement before it was signed, sealed and delivered. Yet we have never seen it and will not until parliament prorogues and the agreement is signed over our heads.
Is this a free parliament or not? Are we conducting business in the way in which it is done in the mother parliament to-day? Does the National Railways belong to the president or to the people of Canada? Is parliament not entitled to this information?
We are 245 representatives of the people of Canada; we are trustees of the people; we are asked on the hustings about the Canadian National Railways and no one cau answer. Is there unnecessary duplication and waste? Are branch lines being built that are not necessary? Does politics enter into the administration of this railway? I do not believe this committee should be appointed. It is not in the public interest that five or six or ten members of parliament should be selected to take our functions away and to deprive us of our right to consider the estimates of this railway. I am interested in the operation and administration of the National Railways and the true and real success of public ownership in this country, and I do not propose as a member of parliament to sit in this House and see a committee of five or six or ten men who may be appointed, who may or may not be in favour of public ownership, take my rights and privileges away from me. The minister, like every other minister, should bring down and explain his estimates to parliament and all the money expended should be in the public accounts. Why should these things be hidden away so that we cannot find out the salaries of these officials or the details of operation and capital account? We know the salary of the Governor General and what is spent on Rideau Hall. The Hon. the Speaker who is the most important public servant we have in this country, who presides over this House, gives us the details of the expenditure for the maintenance of the services of this House.
Surely it is not in the public interest that parliament should have no control over the most important responsibility we have-the National Railways-on which two billion dollars of the taxpayers' money has been spent. What will happen after this committee makes its report? We shall have to sit here and practically take it as read. The minister's estimates are reached at half past one in the morning; only two or three members discuss them; we ask for information and we cannot get it because the minister says: We will ask the head of the railways, and he will say:	It is not in the public
interest. Is it Sir Henry Thornton or this parliament that has the final say as to whether such a matter is in the public interest or not? Is he superior to parliament which appointed him and gave him such great powers? We see instances that indicate that this road is not being administered in a commercial and businesslike way; day after day hon. members ask for information and the minister says:	It is not in the public
interest to furnish it. It is in the public in-
3554	COMMONS
National Railways and Shipping Committee
terest of the Ontario legislature to give information in connection with the HydroElectric and in the interest of the Canadian Pacific Railway to give full information regarding its affairs to its board of directors. You are the board of directors, the trustees of the people of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific in connection with two billion dollars of the taxpayers' money which has been expended on this railway and the conduct of the enterprise. It is not in the public interest that this information should be withheld, and if a vote is taken I intend to register my vote and protest against the lack of responsible government which we have in this parliament to-day.
Is it responsible government that public property amounting to two billion dollars, which is not in my opinion being administered in a commercial, businesslike way, should be taken out of the control of parliament and handed over to a committee which will make a report, whitewash everything, in the dying days of the session when a formal vote will be moved in the House involving millions of dollars, perhaps at the end1 of a last and an all-night session? Off that is the way in which the Canadian National Railways are administered, the sooner we have the end of public ownership, the better. It is not in the public interest that we should hand over our responsibility to a committee. The issue is clear: A vote for this committee to-day is a vote for inefficiency in the administration of this system. It is a vote against public ownership; it is a vote against the trust we have as representatives of the people of Canada, and for that reason I wish to vote against the appointment of this committee as not being in the best interests of the National Railways, of the Canadian merchant marine, of public ownership or of efficiency and economy in our publicly owned railway system.
Mr. A. de WITT FOSTER (Hants-Kings): Mr. Speaker, I do not rise for the purpose of supporting all that has been said by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church); but even if only part of what he says is true, there is much in the contention that he has laid before the House. were told by the minister that when this committee was formed we would be in a position to come before it, ask questions and get information. I can appreciate coming before the committee and being peremptorily told with a wave of the hand: It is not in the public interest to furnish that information.
Is it in the public interest that the people of this country should know whether three or four men from the city of New York who may have been connected with a firm there that went into liquidation, should be given positions in Canada at salaries which, it is reported in the streets, are anywhere from $30,000 to $50,000 a year, when we know there are in this country to-day men 4 p.m. who could be appointed to those jobs at one-half the salaries and who would do just as good work? These matters are in the public interest regardless of whether the management of the National Railways or the government of the day says that it is not in the public interest. I should like to know whether they are paying men three times what they are worth in order to perform jobs which could be very well performed by men raised in this country. If members are to be deprived of the opportunity of securing information in the committee and if when these matters come befroe the House in the last days of the session, and at one o'clock in the morning when everyone is weary, we have perhaps half an hour in which to delve into them-and we are speaking about limiting speeches to thirty or forty minutes-

Hear, hear.
Mr. F'CSTER: Let hon. members limit their own speeches, As regards these particular estimates, if hon. members feel they are not sent here in the interest of the people to discharge their public duties and to take such time as is necessary to do that, they ought not to be here. Mr. Speaker, as chairman for the last two sessions of the committee on National Railways and Shipping, I should like to make a reply to my hon. friend from Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church). I have nothing to say particularly with regard to the willingness of the government to answer certain questions respecting the National Railways; that must be within their judgment. I think they are perfectly right in certain instances to refuse information which might be detrimental to the interests of the National Railways. I can recall very well under the former government that information of a similar character was refused, and I thought the government was right at that time.
There were many protests against the refusal, though.

I know, and I did not agree with those protests altogether. In reply to the statement by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest that the committee does not permit any member to ask questions of those managing the railway, I desire to contradict it flatly. So far as I remember-I am open to correction-no member of the committee was ever refused information by the officials, from Sir Henry Thornton down.

He said members who
were not members of the committee.

I will go further. The meetings of that committee were always open to the members of this House, and there have been instances where members who were not members of the committee itself asked permission of the committee to address certain remarks and questions to those who were present on behalf of the National Railways, and in no case were they refused. I do not think there is any danger whatever, if the committee is reconstituted, that such permission will be refused. In addition to that, all the evidence brought before the committee was printed by permission of the House and was spread upon the records for the information of every member. Something has been said about the Canadian Pacific Railway issuing an illuminating report every year for the information of its shareholders. The National Railways issue a similar financial statement
each year, and I think it is fully as illuminating as that issued by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific management do not spread all the affairs of their railway before the public for their competitors to take advantage of, and I do not think any member of this House who has the real interests of public ownership at heart should ask the management of the National Railways to do something in that particular which the Canadian Pacific management would not do.

Mr. Speaker, I rather concur in this resolution. It seems to me it is quite proper that these estimates should go before a special committee of the House, particularly as the resolution contains this proviso:
That nothing in this resolution shall be construed to curtail in any way the full right of discussion in committee of Supply.
I should like to see the government go a step further and refer all the estimates to a special committee of the House.
Hear, hear.

I believe, Sir, that a great saving of the time of the House could be accomplished in that way. Departmental officers when their estimates were up could be called before that special committee. To me it has always been absurd when a minister of the crown was being asked all sorts of questions, some pertinent, others not, on matters affecting his department-which in many cases he could not be expected to know-to see his deputy, who naturally is familiar with the affairs of his department, compelled to whisper the information to his minister, who repeated it to the House, his deputy not being allowed to give the information direct. I believe in many departments of the government we would get more information and save a great deal of the time of the House if the estimates were dealt with by a special committee.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted to add a word. I had no intention of starting a debate in moving this resolution. I had been informed by members on both sides of the House that the special committee appointed in the past few years to deal with government railway matters had been satisfactory and had been the means of placing much valuable information before the House and the country. The resolution as it stands on the order paper is in exactly the same form as the resolution which was adopted on former occasions. May I point out, Sir, that so far from restricting

National Railways and Shipping Committee
the members of this House, the resolution provides in addition to the ordinary machinery a special committee for the purpose of going into the complex details of National railway financing. It in no way reduces the opportunities of members to secure information; on the contrary, it rather widens them. In this connection I should like to call attention to the proviso referred to by the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn):
Provided, however, that nothing in this resolution shall be construed to curtail in any way the full right of discussion in committee of Supply.
The whole machinery of the House still remains, but in addition to that machinery a small committee of men, selected by agreement between the party whips, is given the special task of going into the very complex matters connected with the administration of our National railway system and the Canadian merchant marine. Surely it is apparent to business men that a small body dealing with these very complex matters can do so more effectively than the whole House.
The matter of refusal of information I endeavoured to deal with yesterday. I admit its difficulty, as every previous Minister of Railwaj'S has admitted it. Paragraph 3 of question 16. I use it merely as an illustration. There may be parts of the question which are quite proper. tions, they can and do, as in the case of all other committees, submit their questions to the parties who are being examined through the medium of a colleague who is a member of the committee.
I moved the resolution, Sir, merely because I am informed that it has been found in the past a satisfactory method of dealing with the affairs of the National Railways and merchant marine. I repeat, the resolution in no way restricts the liberties of hon. members or the ordinary procedure, but rather adds to the machinery of the House and makes it more efficient in dealing with this very important matter.

I would suggest that it is
quite simple to amend the resolution. Surely it is obvious that several members on this side are desirous of appearing before that committee, and if proper representation were given us certain additional members would have an opportunity of putting their questions before that committee.

I do

May I ask the Minister of Railways if he would be good enough to tell me, having doubt-

less considered the matter thoroughly, in what way he thinks the passing of estimates will be furthered by this procedure? I must apologize to m>
hon. friend from Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) in that I omitted to answer his question; it passed from my mind for the moment. Will he repeat it?

Will the minister give a

I think that would be a proper question for this committee to go into. If passes are being issued contrary to the Railway Act I would like to know it, and it would be stopped. But that is not the question my hon. friend asked me before.
Then I am asked as to the functions of the committee and the value to the House of the committee proceedings. That committee can do what this House in committee cannot do, that is, summon before it the railway officials and direct to them all sorts of questions respecting the operation of the people's railway. More than that, many questions which would arise in committee of the Whole if there were no special committee are cleared up in the proceedings of that special committee, without taking up the time of this House. Very much more time is taken up in a body of 245 men, of course, than is taken up by a smaller committee inquiring into the same question. That, I understand, is the facility provided as a result of previous experience. I believe it has generally been regarded as of value to the House to add this committee to the existing machinery of the House, without in any way limiting the right of members in committee of Supply.

I
have had the opportunity of serving on this committee since it was started. It functions well in some directions, and in other directions not so well. that no information is withheld in committee; if he considers the matter I think he will agree that his memory is a little faulty there. In connection with questions of salary, I think my hon, friend will at once agree that information was not forthcoming.

I have heard him state that on various occasions. This session all the committees were struck at the same time, and the number of members on this committee was also accepted at that time. But it happens that the other committees were organized at an earlier stage under that agreement, which was accepted by everybody in the House. Now when this special committee comes to be organized I claim that in justice and fairness to all concerned the agreement, so entered into by the whips and accepted by everybody should prevail.
May I ask the Minister of Justice a question? Does he suggest that any party in this House is bound by the reports of committees? I assume he would say no.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I suggest that in this
instance, as in other instances of arrangements between the whips, it is an honourable agreement and should be accepted and respected by the House.

Are you -going to persist in
ignoring Nova Scotia on this committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the members of my hon. friend's party wish to substitute a member from Nova Scotia in the place of one of the three members from Ontario, the government will be pleased to accept the suggestion. But the point I wish to direct the attention of the House to at the moment illustrates wherein considerations have been taken into account by the striking committee which perhaps we are losing sight of altogether. A special committee cannot exceed 15 in number without the unanimous consent of the House. Now, I venture to say we cannot hope to get such consent to alter this committee as arranged by the whips. That being the fact, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the House pass the resolution, and if when the committee has been appointed there appear to be very strong reasons why its personnel should be altered in any particular, we can then take into consideration anything further that may be necessary to be done.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime
Minister:	Having regard to the vast importance of matters to be dealt with by this committee, does he not really think that he

National Railways and Shipping Committee
could get the consent of the House to double its representation? I think this committee is entirely too small in view of the importance of the business which will come before it. Only those fifteen members on the committee will have the special privilege of getting information and keeping it to themselves. They are not to let it out to any person else.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
let me say to my hon. friend that this committee is different from other committees in that in no manner does the committee take away from the members of the House the right to discuss railway matters in detail. It is simply a committee for sifting information in the first instance, and thereby enabling hon. members to discuss the points they wish to develop further in the House, without bringing in a lot of irrelevant matter, and so save a lot of time that otherwise would be taken up here in seeking information on minor points. It is really a committee for the purpose of saving time.
I appreciate that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If hon. members who are not on the committee wish to appear and get any information, they will De at perfect liberty to do so. The government has no desire in any way to take a stand that cannot be modified. I would suggest that the resolution be permitted to pass, and that the whips of the respective parties should then meet. If they will agree among themselves to allow hon. gentlemen opposite another member, and the remainder of the House another member, we are quite agreeable to accept the arrangement. But I think this should be effected in the same way as the original arrangement-by the whips themselves.

This is an unfortunate misunderstanding and I would propose this as a compromise. Would not the Prime Minister accept a suggestion that the membership, by unanimous consent, be increased by one, that we have the right to name that one, and that he be from Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I made a suggestion, Mr. Speaker, which I think is eminently fair, namely, that the whips themselves should get together and recommend any changes in personnel, seeing that they had to do with the original arrangement. A unanimous suggestion from the whips will receive favourable consideration by the government.

Will the government agree to
accept my suggestion to increase the membership by one?

Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the Prime Min-. ister that to be fair he should allow the resolution to stand and give the whips an opportunity to get together. He must realize that, as a party, his party is not the government. We do not recognize and never will recognize it as such.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I take absolute exception to my hon. friend's statement. I wish him to understand that so far as the government is concerned this is not a question of party at all. It is a question of who is able to command a majority in this House. The present administration is in that position, and it intends to remain there.
Then do away with groups and say:	Here is the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is what we are doing.
Mr. ROSS -(Kingston):	Then let the
government-or what you call the government-demand a majority.

That was done in
January.

It is suggested
that the resolution should be allowed to go through and have the whips consult later, but I think that is quite unfair. Why not withdraw the resolution now and then let the whips get together?
Because the whip representing my hon. friend's party agreed to the list of names contained in the motion. If a change is desired my hon. friends should confer and make a recommendation to the House.

I desire
to speak to this motion very briefly. I quite approve of this method of referring these accounts to a committee, because it does appear to me that we will get better results in this way than by attempting to thresh the matter out in committee of the Whole. But I cannot overlook the fact that this committee is dealing with perhaps the largest and most important matter before the House; the Canadian National Railways extend across Canada, and this committee should be representative of all parts of this country. I think the province of Nova Scotia should be represented, and I think the number suggested, fifteen, is too small.

National Railways and Shipping Committee
I suggest that the House unanimously consent that this number be increased, then let the whips get together and agree upon a selection which will be thoroughly representative of all parts of Canada and of all groups in this House. The committee will then command the confidence of this House and the best possible results will be secured in this very difficult and very important matter.

The
Minister of Justice is generally very fair in his remarks, but though he has referred to this as a gentleman's agreement, even in an agreement of that kind misunderstandings may arise. It is quite clear that there is such a misunderstanding between the government whip and the whip of our party. It is quite clear that parliament is supreme; this question has been referred to parliament and I think even the suggestion of the Prime Minister, that this matter be referred back to the whips, is not quite in order, if I may say so. I think this should be settled by parliament this afternoon.
The injustice we on this side of the House are under has been clearly pointed out. The Minister of Railways has told us that any questions brought up by members not represented on the committee may be referred to those on the committee and that the matters will be discussed. We have sixteen members more than any other group in the House and these sixteen members will be unrepresented. For that reason we should have another representative on that committee. It has also Been pointed out that every province, with the exception of Nova Scotia, has a representative on this committee. That surely is not fair, because I would point out that the Progressive group, having but twenty-two members, have two representatives, whereas the Maritime group having twenty-five members have no representative.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
New Brunswick has
two representatives, Mr. Jones and Mr. Robichaud.
But the members representing Nova Scotia are so vitally interested in this question that they surely should have representation on this committee.

Who suggested
those from the opposite side who should be on the committee?	We know that the
Maritime representation, especially from Nova Scotia, is largely Conservative, and if the Conservative party are desirous of having a
representative of Nova Scotia on this committee it can easily be arranged through the whips.

I think one of the chief difficulties is that this report is not brought into the House for a full discussion. For that reason we should have a full measure of representation in order to see that this report is presented to the House for discussion at an early date.

I can settle that point
in a moment. If hon. members opposite are not prepared to so adjust their representation as to give Nova Scotia a member of the committee, I will undertake that someone on this side of the House will be sufficiently generous to do so.

I am not in a position
to make bargains for our party, but I am pointing out that we are unfairly treated as the situation now stands. I am not content to come to Ontario and ask them to take a man off the committee in order that we may put one of our men in his place. I ask for justice for Nova Scotia.

I would suggest that we take the resolutions up item by item. If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance will address himself to each item as it comes up it will save a great deal of time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is simply an increase of half fi cent in the general tariff to correct a mistake that was made in the Australian agreement in cabling.

I think my hon. friend is wrong in what he tells the House. I think the Australian or New Zealand rate
is half a cent. If my hon. friend looks at the customs tariff he will find under the heading of "Australia and New Zealand, item No. 7," this very item of "fresh meats, n.o.p." and the rate under the British preferential tariff is two cents, under the intermediate two and a half cents, and under the general tariff, three cents, and in the case of Australia and New Zealand half a cent a pound. What is my hon. friend doing? Does he think he is raising the rate of duty on Australian fresh meats from half a cent a pound to two cents? Because if so I do not think he is.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I am raising the general tariff from three cents to three and a half cents so as to give them an additional spread.

While my hon. friend may think that is what he is doing I am afraid that is not the case. I have the statute here and am reading from it. The item he is striking out is:
Meats, British preferential tariff, 2 cents; intermediate tariff, 2$ cents; general tariff 3 cents.
Then the Australian and New Zealand rate is half a cent. I would suggest that my hon. friend look into this question and that in the meantime we report progress.

May I suggest to the Minister of Finance that there is a shortage apparently of these resolutions. I happened to find a copy in my room but I could not get any downstairs. I think there should be some extra copies because other members may have lost the copy they originally received and one cannot form an intelligent idea of what is going on unless he has the resolutions before him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I inform the hon. gentleman that if the files of hon. members are properly kept a copy of these resolutions will be found in the Votes and Proceedings of April 15th. I would suggest that this item be passed.
No, I want to find out what change is really being made here.
